title: The Case of the Misplaced Signpost
markdown:
The signpost was not there.

Teddy Walnut stood in the moonlit clearing with his worn left ear cocked, as if the missing oak might still be hiding behind a better explanation. The arrows that should have offered Berry Bush Lane and Sparkle Stream offered nothing. The woods felt unbalanced in the way a room does when a chair has been taken and no one will admit who sat in it last.

Pearl Decimal snorted, horn scattering moonbeams, mane like spun silver that had opinions about being outdoors. “Must you always wake me at peak luminescence for a vanishing stick?”

Walnut’s stuffing did a small, traitorous flip. He had felt it in the house already: leaves jabbering as if they had lost a map, crickets squabbling over left and right. They had come down the stairs past the snoozing dog, through the ajar back door, into air that smelled of damp earth and jasmine. The ferny woods behind the old walled garden were supposed to be where things stayed put.

They did not.

A squirrel, usually meticulous, was digging where a prize mushroom ought to have been. A ladybug in a ruby shell was climbing a spiderweb upside down, with the grim patience of someone following instructions that had been printed backwards. Dewdrops, if Walnut was not mistaken, had chosen south as a personality.

“Everything’s out of sorts,” he said.

“The woodland’s aesthetic is creatively disrupted,” Pearl replied. “A touch of avant-garde chaos. My presence elevates even bewilderment. Still. If you insist on restoration, lead on. Prevailing winds whisper direction. My internal compass points to instinct.”

“We find the Proper Path marker,” Walnut said. “It holds things together.”

They plunged into ferns that brushed like silk and were not sorry. Cooler air. Moss. Leaves that had finished being leaves.

“Cadoc Owl mentioned a shortcut,” Walnut said. “Special. Through the Whispering Willow Glade. A time for reflection.”

Pearl’s snort was all popping bubbles. “Cadoc Owl. Always cryptic. Special usually means inconvenient, or a long story about acorns. The Thicket of Whispers is far more promising for expedited progress.”

Walnut went to the Glade anyway, because Cadoc had said important and because Pearl’s instinct, though luminous, had never yet replaced a signpost.

The glade was hushed. Pale blue and white bunting hung between gnarled branches, quiet flags, dancing shadows. Not a shortcut. A pause the woods had decorated without asking permission.

“Decorative,” Pearl said, looking down her nose. “Pointless. It doesn’t do anything. And such a muted palette.”

Walnut was already at the ground. Small paw prints. A fluff of moss like a nest against an oak’s roots. And there, leaning at an angle that would have embarrassed a carpenter, the missing signpost.

“It’s here.”

Angry chirps fell out of the leaves. Robins descended, chests puffed, darting and swooping without quite striking. Displeasure with wings.

“Robins,” Pearl sighed, stepping back from a zip of red. “So provincial. They don’t understand urgent woodland restoration.”

Walnut held up his paws. The robins did not stop them so much as stand between them and the moss. A faint sweet scent — young things. “They’re protecting something. Pearl. I don’t think the signpost is lost. I think it was moved.”

The robins settled on a branch, heads cocked, which in robin is as close as you get to go on.

“This isn’t a place for shortcuts,” Walnut said, soft. “Someone used this to make a little fence. For the small ones.”

Pearl looked from bunting to signpost to a tiny chick in the moss. For the first time that night she had nothing decorative to say. She nudged the post with her muzzle until it stood, not in the clearing, but upright enough not to fall on anyone who had only just learned what falling was.

“An ingenious, albeit temporary, architectural solution,” she murmured. “And the bunting… celebratory décor for a hatching. Charming. In its own way.”

A very old badger shuffled from a burrow, rheumy-eyed, tired in the bones. “Oh. Hello. Did you see my little chicks? I moved the old signpost to keep them secure while I went for worms. Didn’t want unwanted visitors. Dangerous world for small things. Especially robins.”

He blinked at the post, now proud, then at the woods, which had begun, faintly, to feel like themselves. “You’ve put it back. Kind. I suppose it belongs in the clearing. Still. My little ones are safe. I do rather like the bunting. Makes them feel special.” A weary nod, and he was gone into the dark of his own door.

Walnut’s smile was the deep kind that does not need an audience. A kind mistake. Not sinister. Worried badgering, if you wanted a joke and had earned one.

Pearl’s horn warmed. “Sometimes the most aesthetically pleasing outcomes arise from unpolished intentions. And the bunting added a certain je ne sais quoi.”

Dawn put pink and gold through the oaks. They set the signpost where Berry Bush Lane and Sparkle Stream could argue in public again. The squirrel returned to mushrooms. The ladybug chose a blade of grass and the correct way up. Dewdrops went back to hanging without politics. The bunting stayed, a leftover celebration no one had the heart to take down.

Walnut and Pearl walked home through jasmine and the last of the cricket arguments, which had become ordinary chirping from sheer embarrassment. The chair, so to speak, was back in the room. The clearing had a heart again. And a teddy with a worn ear, walking beside a unicorn who had learned to stop talking long enough to nudge, found that a satisfying enough end to a night that had started with nothing where a sign ought to be.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
